entry.title: ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama
entry.summary: A Japanese woman and a Korean woman learn they were switched during IVF in an intensely controlled film from Kiyoshi Kurosawa protegé Akira Yamamoto.
entry.content:
“The Intertwining” director Akira Yamamoto was mentored by Kiyoshi Kurosawa, and it shows. Yamamoto is one of many Japanese filmmakers to study under the legendary director of “Cure” and “Tokyo Sonata,” who was a professor at Tokyo University of the Arts from 2005 to 2023. And although he’s not Kurosawa’s most famous pupil — that would be “All of a Sudden”‘s Ryusuke Hamaguchi, whose style is also an influence here — he has clearly taken many lessons on composition and timing from his former teacher. To this end, Yamamoto’s latest feature takes a politically charged family drama and laces it with restrained, but palpable psychological tension, creating a film whose quietest moments are also its most uneasy ones.

Related Stories
Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was
Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut

Yamamoto’s primary tactic for creating this tension is the long take. Shots in this film frequently linger just a few seconds longer than they’re “supposed” to, reflecting the pauses in dialogue scenes where characters choose their words before they speak. Many filmmakers who utilize this tactic like to punctuate these moments with bursts of sudden violence, but aside from the elderly woman collapsing on a city bus who serves as a catalyst for the film’s plot — filmed in a very Kurosawa-esque long shot, by the way — Yamamoto contains himself here, too.

The struggle in “The Intertwining” is all psychological, as the two women who respond to the medical emergency — both medical students, as it turns out — begin to realize that they have a lot in common. Ji-hyun (Jiyoung) is a fifth-year Korean exchange student, although she’s frequently mistaken for Japanese — as Nakano (Karata Erika) notes with surprise when they formally introduce themselves afterwards. They exchange numbers and hang out a few times, eventually figuring out that not only are their parents both in the hospitality business, but they were born at the same clinic around the same time.

Ji-hyun’s parents briefly lived in Tokyo before going back to their home country, discouraged by the discrimination against Koreans that’s still pervasive in Japan today. This becomes extremely important later on as Nakano, who’s never felt at home in her family, decides to test her DNA against those of her parents and brother after learning about DNA sequencing in class. Nakano is both shocked and relieved to discover that the parents she grew up with are not her biological mother and father, and her new friend Ji-hyun supports her as she tries to process these feelings. Then a nurse at the clinic gives Nakano an envelope containing the names of her real parents.

As it turns out, it’s not a coincidence at all that Ji-hyun and Nakano’s parents both sought treatment at the same fertility clinic. Ji-hyun and Nakano were both the product of IVF, and their embryos were implanted in their respective mothers on the same day. Except the doctor made a mistake, meaning that Nakano is actually Korean, and Ji-hyun — who’s also faced prejudice for her ethnicity while living in Japan — is actually Japanese. The scene where the clinic’s current head tries to explain what went wrong more than 20 years ago contains another of the movie’s rare outbursts, as Nakano’s father angrily confronts the doctor for “putting a Korean embryo into [his] wife.” In his mind, this is the worst betrayal of them all, and the way he prioritizes his family’s honor over his daughter’s happiness is one of the reasons why Nakano feels no guilt about leaving him behind.

Ji-hyun, on the other hand, loves her family very much. She does not want to become Japanese, and the political undertones of their respective identity crises are one of the film’s most crackling unspoken undercurrents. Ji-hyun pities Nakano, but maintains boundaries between them even after the two go to South Korea to visit Ji-hyun’s warm and supportive family at their picturesque restaurant by the sea. By this point, the bubble of unspoken words between these two women is straining with tension. But Yamamoto is too subtle, and too savvy, of a director to let it burst.

Instead, we’re left with some challenging questions about identity, and what makes a person who they truly are. Although it’s the central conflict, the mix-up at the clinic is not the only outrageous coincidence in this movie, and “The Intertwining” could have been even stronger with a slightly tighter narrative focus. Still, it’s a testament to Yamamoto’s filmmaking that these feel less like plot contrivances and more like the invisible reverberations of fate.

“The Intertwining” does require patience and active engagement, both of which are made possible by committed, but controlled performances from Jiyoung and Karata, who also starred in Hamaguchi’s “Asako I & II.” One could easily imagine the premise of this movie as the stuff of Sirkian melodrama. But Yamamoto asks his leads to internalize these big emotions rather than externalize them through his filmmaking, and the controlled intensity shown by all three key players is key to what makes “The Intertwining” work.

Grade: B+

“The Intertwining” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

entry.title: Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was
entry.summary: Billy Evans answered questions from 'You Can See Everything' fans in an AMA on his X account.
entry.content:
One of 2026’s distinct pleasures (for lack of a better word) has been getting to know Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’ life partner and power of attorney holder who becomes the primary focus of “You Can See Everything.” Evans and Holmes have two kids together and are working to launch a new blood testing startup in the vein of Theranos. While Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film begins as a relatively straightforward documentary about Holmes and Evans’ life in San Diego during the last month before she reported to federal prison, it spirals into a larger investigation into Evans’ influence on Holmes and the nature of their partnership.

Related Stories
Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut
Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch

It’s a three-hour movie, but you’re not alone if you left with unanswered questions about the couple. Fortunately, Evans himself is still active as ever on X — both his own account, and the one he runs for Holmes. And on Monday, November 2, Evans spent some time answering questions from fans… everything was on the table other than his caveat that every question “needs to be legally permissible.”

He tried to clarify some of the film‘s more confusing moments, including his frequent onscreen sniffing, which he chalked up to allergies. As for rumors that cocaine might be to blame, Evans wrote, “Never been a fan.”

Evans also went into detail about his relationship with Holmes, denying that he has any real control over her but admitting that he’s still romantically crazy about her. He noted that he misses her presence and touch so much that the Theranos founder “should qualify as a medically necessary prescription.”

Perhaps most importantly, he addressed the burning question of what his cousin’s “thing” was. Early in the film, Evans abruptly cuts off a conversation with Fielder on the beach when the topic turns to his family’s wealth by vaguely stating that he’s late for his cousin’s thing. Evans claimed that it was a marriage proposal, and implied that he ended up getting there in time.

And of course, the shower scene came up. Evans pushed back on the idea that he wanted to do full frontal nudity in the documentary, dismissing that suggestion from a fan as a “false narrative.” He also linked to a PEOPLE story that claims he was “violated” by the scene and wrote “trust the sources.”

Evans also did not limit himself to questions about the film. Other AMA questions focused on his cultural tastes, and Evans used the platform to express his love for Chappell Roan, Kendrick Lamar, Charlie Kirk, and Taylor Swift (he said he bought Holmes’ engagement ring at the Reputation tour merch booth).

Fielder and Oppenheimer’s film makes it clear that nobody can really see everything in a documentary, but Evans appears committed to proving that you can post everything if you try hard enough.

entry.title: Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut
entry.summary: Jordan Firstman discusses 'Club Kid,' his tender feature debut about queer nightlife and chosen family. World premiere Cannes 2026. Interview.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. A24 will release “Club Kid” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

The official Cannes synopsis for “Club Kid” is almost suspiciously vague: “A washed-up party promoter is forced to turn his life around when an unexpected visitor arrives.” Hmm…

Technically, that’s true. But it’s also the kind of carefully evasive logline you can only use if you’re an artist as charismatic and cunning as Jordan Firstman. A writer, actor, singer, comedian, and now debut feature filmmaker, Firstman has spent years making audiences feel like they know everything about him without fully surrendering the parts of himself that might actually hurt.

Related Stories
Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch
To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

“People have trouble metabolizing me for a lot of different reasons, ” Firstman told IndieWire, ahead of his dazzling feature film’s world premiere at the Cannes Film Festival on May 15. “I think I remind them of someone they know, but also someone they don’t know. Or someone who deserves things, but also someone they went to high school with who’s just an annoying gay guy. Perception is weird.” 

For years, Firstman’s public persona has existed somewhere between chaotic queer oracle and self-aware caricature — whether through his hilariously unhinged Instagram comedy, his writing and acting work on shows like “Search Party,” “The Other Two,” and “I Love LA,” or his caustic self-portrayal in Sebastián Silva’s “Rotting in the Sun,” which debuted at Sundance in 2023. 

“I wanted the thing I did after that to be a bit softer and more like a version of me that I knew, but other people didn’t,” Firstman said. “There was a lot on me in that movie in terms of persona and people thinking about me in a certain type of way.” (Suffice to say, Firstman spends much of “Rotting in the Sun” cartoonishly chasing attention and ketamine on the beach.) 

The “Club Kid” filmmaker also wrote the viral Laura Dern tribute that was performed by the Gay Men’s Chorus of Los Angeles at the 2020 Spirit Awards (“Top five moments of my life,” Firstman joked), which helped carve out space for his unique voice in Hollywood. Sliding effortlessly from incisive observer to chaotic flirt to exhausting narcissist, Firstman is never not in on the joke. But it took until now for him to finally explore what happens when that cyclical sense of self-parody stops working as armor and starts feeling like a weight.

“I didn’t want to win anyone over anymore,” Firstman said of his mentality heading into this project. “All I could do was tell the story I wanted to tell in the way that I wanted to tell it.” 

A funny and melancholy look at one man’s deep feelings of isolation, appropriately set against the fast-changing experience of modern queer nightlife, “Club Kid” stars Firstman as Peter, a gay New York party fixture whose chemically accelerated existence is interrupted by the sudden arrival of a child he never knew he had. That setup could easily lend itself to a broader (read: straighter) comedy, but Firstman’s soulful consideration of finding both family and purpose hits a much more sensitive frequency than that. 

Not nearly as interested in punishing Peter for his messiness as it is in helping explain why he built his life this way in the first place, “Club Kid” draws a lot of its tension from the inherent conflict between the pursuit of shallow visibility and the fundamental need for more meaningful types of intimacy. The damage and acceptance that kind of internal contradiction can bring to a person over an extended period runs through every frame of Firstman’s film, and the result feels less like a conventional dramedy than a decade-long discovery unfolding in real time.

With a slick, feel-good opening scene that smartly orients the entire experience, “Club Kid” charts Peter’s evolution from the mid-2010s into the spiritually scorched present with merciless specificity. 

“I remember that era was the start of Europe coming to America gay-wise,” Firstman said. “Dark rooms were not really a thing before that. It was Molly, and maybe some coke, and that was kind of it.” Then came COVID. “I said this famously in the pandemic, but it’s like, you take sex away from gay people for a month, and they’ll make up for it for the next five years.” 

According to Firstman, as the substances changed in many American clubs, so did the emotional atmosphere surrounding some parts of LGBTQ culture. “In 2020 and 2021, K got really big. Then G started in 2022. Then, the last couple years, the Mephedrone, the 3MMC, and 4MMC,” he explained. “You look around, and you see zombies where it should be a community. And sometimes that still feels like your community? It just changed.”

The brilliance of “Club Kid” lies in Firstman’s refusal to flatten those realities into an easy morality. His film understands the air of danger, loneliness, and instability often inherent in queer spaces — while warmly demonstrating why countless people keep returning to them anyway. No one in Firstman’s script is reduced to a victim or cautionary tale, least of all Firstman. And in the end, even his harshest skeptics will struggle to shake the affection they’ll feel for a character who has spent years finding and losing himself under the same strobe lights.

“Even when you strip back the surface layer of the drugs and the afters going on all weekend, beneath it is a bunch of queer people who are funny and sensitive and broken in some ways and artistic and just fully whole,” Firstman said. “That’s what I wanted to show.”

The heart of “Club Kid” is in Peter’s relationship with his son, played by newcomer Reggie Absolom, whom Firstman discovered after watching hundreds of audition tapes out of London. “I remember seeing the thumbnail and being like, ‘Please be able to act, please be able to act, because that’s him,’” Firstman said. “Then I met him, and we went for ice cream and talked about music. I sent all the kids the playlist I wrote the movie to. Reggie loved Massive Attack.”

At several points throughout our conversation, Firstman became emotional discussing his kid scene partner and their film’s larger themes of innocence, queer identity, and the cruel impermanence of self-perception. One moment in particular, in which Reggie bonded with the movie’s ensemble cast of queer and trans performers, overwhelmed him. 

“For the rest of his life now he’s going to love trans people because he got to see how funny and creative [they are], and listen to music with them and joke around with them,” Firstman said, trailing off emotionally. “I think that’s the beauty of this story.”

That softness feels revelatory coming from an artist who has so often weaponized irony and overstimulation as an entertainment strategy. Moments earlier, Firstman had been casually breaking down the social consequences of post-pandemic partying and joking about his “level of hotness.” Then, he was crying and discussing chosen family.

“Everything shows on me,” Firstman laughed, describing the quality as a “gift and a curse.” “Maybe people have complicated feelings toward me because I can’t really hide anything.” 

What makes “Club Kid” as hysterical as it is devastating? Its writer/director’s keen understanding that exposure and vulnerability are not the same thing. Peter has spent years being looked at — desired, consumed, partied with, projected onto — without ever fully learning how to let himself be seen. The arrival of his son has the power to change that, and viewers, too.

“A lot of queer people lose their innocence young and then go straight into this world that can be debaucherous,” Firstman said. “They don’t get a chance to go back to that. Then they don’t have kids. I think for a lot of people, kids bring out their inner child in ways they never expected.” 

Speaking with IndieWire, the filmmaker repeatedly returned to the idea that queer adulthood can feel like an endless negotiation between freedom and self-destruction. But even at its saddest, “Club Kid” remains startlingly sweet. Firstman has an almost anthropological understanding of the contemporary queer social scene in New York, and his movie is packed with the kind of hyper-specific observations that can only come from somebody who has spent years studying how humor functions as both a tool for connection and an often unwieldy defense mechanism.

“I’ve softened a lot in the process of making it,” Firstman said. “I think I’ve struggled so much with my queerness, not in a traditional way, but more in the actual community and having so many mixed feelings about it. Because it isn’t simple. It’s very rich and full. And I think all this [with ‘Club Kid’] happened at the right time and when I could handle it in my life.” 

For all its scenes of spiraling, “Club Kid” is ultimately about the terrifying decision to let yourself be loved without performing for acceptance first. The fact that Firstman can communicate a concept so psychologically naked suggests the arrival of a major new auteur unafraid to move forward on his own terms. “Club Kid” is the most honest Firstman appearance to date. 

“Club Kid” premieres at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival in the Un Certain Regard section.

entry.title: Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch
entry.summary: Netflix launched a new AI Discover feature to help audiences find things they want to watch more easily.
entry.content:
You too, Netflix? Netflix’s whole thing has been that its algorithm was designed in such a way that it knows what you’ll want to watch, that even small shows with no hype or stars like “Baby Reindeer,” “Adolescence,” “Squid Game,” “Ginny and Georgia,” or even “Stranger Things” once upon a time can turn into massive, organic hits. They call it the “Netflix Effect” for a reason.

But even Netflix has had trouble keeping people consistently engaged and in getting them to find that next show or film. Last month it overhauled its creative leads to meet that challenge, so it is turning to where so many other companies have turned to shake things up: AI.

Related Stories
To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

Netflix today launched AI Discover, which is a new tab on the streamer’s TV app where you can ask an AI assistant to help you narrow down a selection based on what you say you’re in the mood to watch. Fortunately Netflix didn’t do the Meta thing and come up with some cuddly meeple to be your virtual assistant.

The tool is built around themes, in which you select from a range of themes, each of which is previewed via a clip from a show or movie. You can say I want to watch “Something Light” or “Scare Me” or ask for something for families, something that’s popular, or something quick, to name a few options. The AI will give you recommendations, it will allow you to refine your selections further and you can continue doom scrolling, and you can finally “Tune Your Recommendations” to either keep a recommendation or tell the AI to not recommend it again.

What this is not is an AI chat bot. You don’t even type anything into it (TV remotes are sometimes hard for that), just pick from some pre-selected options until you get what you want. The AI also though won’t be available on kids profiles, for now it’s not available on mobile, just TVs, and the data collected won’t be used to inform future content decisions for what Netflix produces.

While this could be seen as just a fancy new search function with an AI label, Netflix clarifies that this is new tech they’ve been building with a predictive intelligence model that responds in real time and continues learning based on your preferences. It’s a function on top of the existing search that’s a bit more refined.

For now, AI Discover is only available for a handful of U.S. members who are using it in English and on supported TVs, but it’ll open wider in the coming weeks. The AI Discover function is indicated with a red gem icon and a “New” label on the top of your screen.

entry.title: To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’
entry.summary: Heder takes on a seminal moment in the life of the remarkable disability activist Judy Heumann. It's risky, populated by disabled actors, & worth it.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release “Being Heumann” in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.]

After I watched Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in the weeks leading up to its world premiere as the opening night film at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, I had a long list of things to talk to the filmmaker about.

Top of that list: curb cuts.

Curb cuts — those graded concrete ramps at the edge of sidewalk corners that allow anyone and anything with wheels to glide gently onto the street below — aren’t really the sort of thing most people think about. But if you need them, if you’re in a wheelchair or pushing a stroller or dragging a heavy suitcase, they’re tough not to think about. It’s hard to jump off a curb if you can’t, well, jump. At best, you need help. At worst, you just can’t do it.

Related Stories
How to Make IndieWire a Preferred Source on Google
Taika Waititi’s Delusional ‘Klara and the Sun’ Instagram Post Exemplifies the Dangers of a Growing Divide Between Critics and Artists in the Digital Age

That’s where Heder’s film opens.

Starring British actress Ruth Madeley as the iconic activist Judith Heumann, “Being Heumann” wastes no time putting our star in the middle of a busy New York City street, with not a curb cut to be seen. She doesn’t really have a choice. A wheelchair user for most of her life (Heumann contracted polio as a toddler), Heumann grew into the “Mother of the Disability Rights Movement,” and the film finds her at an important crossroads.

First, she needs to be able to navigate the world around her, which was simply not built for her. No curb cuts.

But things are changing. When the film begins, the first U.S. federal civil rights protection for people with disabilities, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, has been signed, but no one is putting it into actual action. Heumann set out to change that. The film jumps ahead four years, following Heumann as she leads hundreds of fellow activists and disabled people into a massive protest, including a historic sit-in in the San Francisco Federal Building that lasted a month.

It’s real history, but it’s also rousing and funny and entertaining. And deeply human.

It is, of course, very similar to Heder’s previous film, “CODA,” which followed a deaf family and their one hearing child as they navigated a world not built for them. The film premiered at the 2021 Sundance Film Festival, where it proved to be a huge crowdpleaser (no easy feat, as that edition of the festival was held entirely online). A year later, it won Best Picture, changing Heder’s life forever.

After her big Oscar win, Heder had some immediate needs to meet. “I had worn these high heels for so many hours the night of the Oscars that my toes went numb, and it took maybe two months to come back to life and have feeling in my toes again,” she told IndieWire with a laugh. “But there was a moment of recovery, not just from the energy that it took to go through an awards campaign, to do a Q&A every night, to fly all over the world with the movie, but also the adrenaline leaving your body, which was a very intense feeling.”

Choosing what project she’d take on next was also top of mind for Heder, who admitted that it took awhile for her to get back into the process of actually creating after spending more than a year sharing “CODA” with the world. That was intense, too.

“It’s shocking moment as a filmmaker, because suddenly there’s a bunch of eyes on you that were never there before,” she said. “‘What are you going to do next?’ and ‘How are you going to follow that up?’ It took some time for me to tap back into why I tell stories and what moves me. I developed a lot of projects. I had maybe five different movies that I was developing or writing or overseeing a writer on and didn’t really know which one would come together first.”

And then there was “Being Heumann,” which Heder has been working on in earnest for about five years. She first met Heumann at Sundance in 2021, when Nicole Newnham and James LeBrecht’s documentary “Crip Camp” premiered, in which the irrepressible Heumann appeared as a young woman. (Heder also co- wrote the script alongside Rebekah Taussig, based on Heumann’s autobiography.)

“It was before ‘CODA’ had come out, it was before I had taken the whole Oscar ride,” Heder said. “I had been drawn to this story because it was a great story, long before I was thinking about what’s the right move in the industry or how do you follow up a film that goes on to do [win Best Picture]. It was just very close to my heart.”

There was also Judy Heumann. Heder said she knew from her very first meeting with Heumann that she wanted to make a film about her. She hadn’t even been aware of Heumann until she saw the documentary, and then? She couldn’t take her eyes off her.

“There’s a scene where she’s yelling about lasagna in the cafeteria at summer camp, and I was like, ‘Who is this woman?’ She looked like she was conducting a senate hearing, but she’s talking about what they’re going to have for dinner,” Heder said. “I was very intrigued by her as a character, but I felt like there was a deadly version of this story, which would’ve been a traditional biopic.”

Heder had been working with Heumann for nearly two years before Heumann died in March 2023. Heder said she had a “a very strong feeling that Judy died having chosen me to make this movie and tell the story, and so there was a sense of responsibility to her and her legacy.”

There was also, by her own telling, “a little bit of fear of, if I follow up ‘CODA’ with another film that’s about disability, are people going to put me in that box? But after ‘CODA,’ I had a rare moment of power in the industry where a lot of people wanted to make what I wanted to make. There was a moment where I could have used that capital to go make a Marvel movie and get a big paycheck and move out of my small home in Eagle Rock or use the capital to try to tell the hardest story I could imagine trying to tell and probably a film that not a lot of people would’ve financed or gotten behind.”

She went with the latter. “I knew it was going to be an all-disabled cast with a lot of new actors and without movie star names, and it was a period piece and it was more expensive than your average indie movie,” Heder said. “So it felt like if there was ever a moment that I could push it through to tell this story, that was the moment I was in.”

And while it was not an automatic yes from Apple, which also distributed “CODA,” Heder said, “They believed in the movie for sure, and they believe in me as a filmmaker. But, on paper, this movie is a challenging film.” Those challenges went beyond the already-daunting needs around casting.

“Yes, on one hand, it’s a story about a disability rights activist in the 1970s,” Heder said. “It was important to me that the film not feel like ‘eat your spinach’ or that it was not there to educate people on something important that they should know about. What I pitched to Apple is ‘I want to make “Dog Day Afternoon” with disabled people. I want to make a story that has a lot of momentum and humor.’ These people were building sex tents in the hallway, they were smoking pot, and the Black Panthers showed up! That’s a movie that I think will be fun to watch and joyful and entertaining. They understood not just that I was trying to tell the story, but the way I was trying to tell it.”

While Heder eschewed any “eat your spinach” angles, she’s still very passionate about sharing the incredible impact of Heumann’s work in the disabled community. “Most disabled people at the time didn’t even really understand that they could demand to be a part of society or demand equal rights,” Heder said. “There was a feeling of, ‘Well, your body is broken, so you don’t deserve to leave your house,’ and I think a lot of people had internalized that, and Judy awakened that understanding in a lot of people.”

Judy Heumann’s story also awakened a different understanding in Heder herself. The film doesn’t canonize Heumann, instead showing her as dedicated leader who is also prickly, brash, and set in her ways. Heder didn’t just want to tell a story about a leader, but what it actually takes to be a leader and continue growing in that role.

“There are so many tropes around disability, so the idea of meeting this young person who feels invisible and finds her voice and becomes an activist and comes into her power was the more expected story,” the filmmaker said. “But meeting someone who is at the height of their power, who has this radical empathy where she’s fighting for people to be seen and heard, and yet has a really hard time seeing and hearing and including other people, was a much more interesting character arc. On one hand, Judy is fighting for this group of people to be seen as human. But being a human on a very basic, connective level? Saying thank you to the people who are helping you, being kind, putting the people first? That was also a journey Judy had to go on.”

There’s a moment in the third act of the film when Judy is unable to physically be at the San Francisco sit-in. She not only has to trust that the more soft-spoken Kitty Cone (Madeline Delp), who has become her closest confidant, can keep the sit-in going in her absence, but she must also say that to her. You can see how hard that is for her, but how revelatory, too.

“I do think, as a director — and not to say ‘woman director,’ because I hate constantly qualifying director with my gender — there was a feeling when I started out as a young woman that I had to always have the answers, always seem in control and I knew what I was doing because if I expressed any self-doubt or any waffling, it would be perceived as ‘she doesn’t know what she’s doing,’” Heder said. “It took me a long time to get comfortable enough with my skillset, with my ability to be on a set, and go, ‘I actually don’t know. I actually don’t know where we should put the camera right now. What do you think?’”

Casting that kind of powerful person to portray Judy was charged on many levels. There was no question that Heder would find a disabled actress, but how do you cast someone to be Judith Heumann, so naturally without peer? Heder had worked with the real Judy for years. She knew all the important people in her life.

“There was an intimacy that you almost never have with your lead character,” Heder said. “Yes, Judy was a wheelchair user, but that was one element of her identity. It was also about Judy’s blunt sense of humor, Judy’s directness, Judy’s drive, Judy’s sense of humor, and all of those qualities were things that I was looking for. It was trying to find someone that physically resembled her, who also could embody her energy, which was very specific.”

She likes to joke that her casting directors, Bernie Telsey and Adam Caldwell, had to take on the “casting Olympics, because every character was a unicorn.” “I was like, ‘Hey, go find me a 19-year-old Black blind man who can sing, who has this relentless optimism and just embodies Dennis Billups,’” Heder said with a laugh. (They did, with first-time actor Charlie Rush-Reese, a gem in a sea of them.)

She found Madeley in a slightly different way. “I was working with a deck designer to put images together when I was trying to get the movie greenlit at Apple, and he was British, and he said, ‘This character really reminds me of this actress, Ruth Madeley. Do you know her work?,’” she said. “I didn’t know her, but she was in this film called ‘Then Barbara Met Alan,’ and I watched the film and I could see exactly what he was talking about. She has an earthy, wry humor, and she exudes intelligence and has this big well of emotion and vulnerability.”

Still, Heder said with a laugh, she didn’t make it easy on Madeley. “Ruth had done so much work before I ever met her, but I put her through the ringer. I auditioned her many times,” Heder said. “I saw many, many actors for that role, and she truly won that part. I knew it was going to be an incredibly difficult film to make, and I felt I really had a partner with her. Even aside from performance, which is the most important thing, having a true collaborator in your lead actor is invaluable as a director.”

Heder’s film is filled with incredible star turns by a number of new (and, in some cases, brand-new) performers. Among their ranks is, however, one very recognizable name: Mark Ruffalo, cast here as Joseph Califano, the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. He’s the guy who needs to sign the meaningful regulations that would put 504 into actual action. And, for most of the film’s running time, he refuses to do it. He’s the bad guy of the story, sort of, and to have an outspoken activist like Ruffalo in that role adds real dimension to the part.

“Mark is someone who has been unafraid in his life to be principled and stand by those principles, whatever the cost,” Heder said. “And Califano was someone who really considered himself a good guy and had, throughout his career, protected the Selma March, pushed forth the Great Society Program, had stood with the students at Kent State, and really felt like ‘I’m on the right side of history.’”

When the film begins, he has just started to work for President Jimmy Carter, and the pressure is on. The president gave Califano a strict mandate: cut the federal budget by $3 billion. He was less than three months into his job when the sit-ins began. The moment he signed the 504 regulations, he’d have 60 days to enact the necessary changes to meet its requirements. And they would cost $3 billion.

“The more I read about Califano, the more I felt like you could tell this story from his perspective, you could absolutely understand that he was between a rock and a hard place, but that’s when people’s principles are actually tested,” Heder said. “In my first meeting with Mark, he was talking about fear, and there are a lot of politicians now who are living in a state of fear, whether it’s their reelection, whether it’s losing money that backs their campaign or offending lobbyists or constituents.”

She added, “The reality is, the movie is not speaking to a mustache-twirling villain who is out to make life hard for disabled people, it’s speaking to the good guys who are stuck in inaction because it feels too hard or too scary. That’s very timely for me, because we all have something to protect that you risk by going out on a limb and announcing what you believe in. There’s a lot of fear right now, and we see it real time, and so there are actual repercussions to speaking up and standing by your morals.”

Inaction isn’t Heder’s bag. In making a film like “Being Heumann,” which is literally about the fight for accessibility, there was no question she had to build a production that was comfortable, creative, and open for all. That didn’t scare her. Why should it? It’s attainable.

“With ‘CODA,’ we were trying to make a set accessible to a deaf cast, which was one very specific thing, and so it was about communication and ‘where do we put interpreters?’ and ‘how do I call action and how do I call cut?,'” she said. “But it was all working toward meeting a very specific set of needs on this movie because it was cross-disability. Someone who is paraplegic has very different needs than someone who is an ambulatory wheelchair user versus someone who lives in chronic pain. It was about making a set that is accessible to a deaf cast at the same time that you’re making that set accessible to a blind actor. And we didn’t know what we didn’t know.”

Heder and her crew had to figure out how to navigate everything from ramps to scripts. How do you do a table read with a blind actor? How do you do ADR when they can’t see their own mouth moving? How many braille scripts do you need? Will audio earpieces help? How many interpreters need to be there for the deaf performers?

“At every stage of the process, we were coming up against these hurdles that were unexpected, even though we had built an accessibility team and we had really done our best to do intake forms for every actor to understand what their needs were on set,” Heder said. “A lot of our cast had never been in a movie before, or some of them were non-actors and so didn’t even know to ask, didn’t even know what they would need to ask, because it’s very different to say, ‘Yes, I’m fine in a vintage wheelchair, but are you fine in a vintage wheelchair for 12 hours?’ Because that’s what a movie set is. There was a lot of real time adjusting that had to happen and problem-solving in the moment. It never stopped.”

Heder is clear, however: this was worth it. “I never want people to take from this at all that it is too hard to work with a disabled actor, I think it’s about knowing what you need,” she said. “Once we figured out what people needed, it really did flow and run as any other set would. It was just a learning curve figuring out what those accommodations were. Judy impulsively led a hundred disabled people into this federal building, many of whom went in without their attendants or their caregivers and then had to figure out how to survive in this building over this 30 days. They all had to find their superpower in their own disability.”

The challenges they faced (and overcame) also helped align them with what Judy Heumann and the rest of the protestors felt during the sit-in. “When I interviewed Dennis Billups, who is blind, he said he was standing lost outside the protest, and he offered to push a wheelchair user if they would guide him into the building,” Heder said. “There was all of this interdependence that started to happen in the protest that was about survival, and that happened in real life on our set, where our cast started jumping in to fill each other’s needs in a way that is very hard to describe and was incredibly profound.”

I mentioned how touching it is to see the way that Heder shows that on the screen, that everyone is useful and that everyone has something that they can do, when she added a compelling corollary. “Not only is everyone useful, but everyone needs help,” Heder said. “Everyone needs help. It’s not just the disabled cast that needed help. There were moments where my non-disabled cast needed help, and there were moments where people on the crew needed help.”

She continued, “It’s like the same way when I was a new mom and I was pushing a stroller around the city, ‘thank God for curb cuts,’ or getting off the subway in New York City and having to lug a stroller up the stairs, ‘thank God for the elevator.’ We all have these moments where you understand that accessibility helps everybody. We built ramps onto our set from every direction, and the grips were like, ‘Thank you. We are lugging thousands of pounds of equipment, and this is the first set I’ve been on where there are ramps everywhere you look, and we can wheel that stuff up.'”

It’s the exact lesson we see in the film, and one that people still need to be reminded of: we can make the world a better place for everyone, but we have to work together.

“I remember there being a big scandal or pushback when there were directors who came out and said, ‘I don’t allow chairs on my set,’ and what you are saying through that,” Heder said. “I understand the intention, which is ‘I want people committed and energized and not kicking back and not participating.’ However, you are also saying that you are not inviting anybody onto your set that cannot stand for 12 hours. … When you refuse to provide any accommodations, you are shutting off an avenue to so much talent and creativity.”

Heder added, “That was the thing I really felt more than anything on this. It was profound to me that what Judy did with these protestors, how this group of people physically changed our world. It’s things that we all take for granted, now that there are curb cuts or Zoom or FaceTime or even texting. All of these moments of innovation came out of inclusiveness that are now accepted as our reality.”

Thank God for curb cuts.

“Being Heumann” will premiere at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.

entry.title: How to Make IndieWire a Preferred Source on Google
entry.summary: How to set IndieWire as a preferred news source on Google.
entry.content:
Do you rely on IndieWire‘s film and TV coverage? If so, please consider taking a moment to ensure you never miss an important story via Google‘s new Preferred Sources feature.

Choosing IndieWire as a preferred source ensures that Google will prioritize IndieWire stories in all of your queries, including traditional searches, Discover, and AI Overviews. Whether you’re searching for movie release dates, TV recommendations, or the latest breaking news, you’ll have access to IndieWire’s reporting and analysis.

If you want to add IndieWire as one of your preferred sources, you can either click this link, click the “Add Us As a Preferred Google Source” button at the top of this article, or manually adjust your preferences by following the instructions below.

Search Google for Any Film or TV-Related Subject

First, head to Google.com and search for any entertainment topic. A movie, a TV show, or a film festival will all work perfectly.

Click the “Customize” Icon to the Right of “Top Stories”

Head to the “Top Stories” section of your results that links to news websites. In the top right corner, you’ll see a starred icon that says “Customize.” Click it.

Search for Preferred Sources and Type “IndieWire”

Clicking the customize button will open a new search bar that asks you to type in your preferred sources. That’s where you can add IndieWire.

Reload Your Results

Once you’ve selected IndieWire as a preferred source, simply click the “Reload Results” button in the bottom right corner, and you’ll be all set!

entry.title: Taika Waititi’s Delusional ‘Klara and the Sun’ Instagram Post Exemplifies the Dangers of a Growing Divide Between Critics and Artists in the Digital Age
entry.summary: Why Taika Waititi's 'Klara and the Sun' Instagram post shows the dangers of a divide between critics and artists in the digital age
entry.content:
I’ve seen enough: Taika Waititi is no longer riffing on a level that is frickin’ sublime. A quick update for those of you who don’t get your news from DiscussingFilm and/or obsessively listen to “Who? Weekly” in order to keep tabs on Rita Ora: On Saturday afternoon, writer-director Taika Waititi opened Instagram and posted — to his grid! — a less than equanimous reaction to the reviews of his new motion picture “Klara and the Sun,” which was in the process of making less money per screen during its second weekend than the average movie theater employee. It wasn’t the most embarrassing self-own of the pre-midterms weekend (that honor belongs to Michigan congresswoman Hayley Stevens, who committed political suicide on live TV with Anderson Cooper), but I’d argue that Waititi’s faux pas has more to say about how the reality distortion field of today’s media landscape has made it all too easy for highly visible people to misperceive the world around them in a crisis.

Related Stories
Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break
‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement

“I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years,” the director wrote under an image celebrating the 53-point mismatch between the film’s audience and critics scores on Rotten Tomatoes. “But I do listen to the people, so this Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus became critics. The same people who also hated ‘Jojo Rabbit 😂 🤷🏽‍♂️.’ Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.🗑️😢🫶🏽.”

When I saw that his post had been modified, I assumed that Waititi had deleted the part where he wrote “and another thing: I’m not mad. Please don’t put in the newspaper that I got mad.” In truth, he had simply tweaked the bit where it said that “sad lost souls” like me had settled as critics. Good note! Much as fallen angels plummet from the heavens before landing in the depths of Hell to anguish for all eternity, critics don’t settle for a life of press screenings so much as we pathetically free fall into it, plummeting from the sacred highs of making “Thor: Love & Thunder” to the wretched lows of watching it. It’s that natural eye for editing that explains why “Next Goal Wins” felt like it had been cut with a soccer cleat.

Of course, I don’t take any of this too personally. (Don’t you dare fucking put in the newspaper that I got mad.) For one thing, I was actually quite tolerant of “Thor: Love & Thunder,” if only because I believe that casting Christian Bale as a guy named “Gorr the God Butcher” in and of itself makes that movie better than most of what Marvel was pumping out at the time. For another thing, I haven’t even seen “Klara and the Sun” — not because I was busy when it screened here, or because I live in one of the many countries where its release has been canceled on account of the movie’s supposed awfulness and verifiable lack of public interest, but rather because I adore the Kazuo Ishiguro novel on which it’s based, and I was convinced that hiring the director of “Jojo Rabbit” to adapt such a poignant tale of loss and brokenness would be like hiring Peter Farrelly to remake “The Remains of the Day.” Except worse, because I’ve always felt like the Merchant Ivory version of that book could have used a few gratuitous jokes about Anthony Hopkins’ swollen balls.

The truth is that the perceived quality of Waititi’s film is irrelevant to what I found interesting about his Instagram post, in much the same way as its quality is seemingly irrelevant to everything else as well. And in much the same way as the perceived quality of Waititi’s other films is irrelevant to the hissy fit he decided to throw about this one. Are “the same people who also hated ‘Jojo Rabbit’” in the room with us? Because that Oscar-winning movie is sitting at 81 percent on Rotten Tomatoes (Certified Fresh™!). OK sure, I hated it, but, as we’ve previously established, I am quite literally not “the same people” who hated “Klara and the Sun.”

On the other hand, I would very much consider myself to be among the large cohort of critics who adored Waititi’s earlier features like “Hunt for the Wilderpeople,” “What We Do in the Shadows,” and “Eagle vs. Shark.” I suppose I could look up the aggregator metrics for those movies as well, but there isn’t any need — that most of the people reading this article have even heard of such modest Kiwi treasures is testament enough to the groundswell of critical support they received around the world. Perhaps, if he’d read a review in the last 15 years, Waititi might have been able to put that together for himself.

But that’s OK. As a public-facing person whose work offers considerably more fodder for mockery than praise (both by virtue of its nature, and also by that of the je ne sais quoi I bring to the job), I would never sincerely begrudge an artist for not wanting to read their own press. Especially now. Perhaps it used to be possible for celebrities to engage with such things in good faith (it was certainly easier in the days when pans were only found in newspapers, and personal attacks limited to their gossip columns), but the internet is a machine designed to make you hate yourself even more than you hate everyone else, and even our finest “anti-hate satires” have proven incapable of solving the problem.

For some folks, especially those with much greater profiles than my own, the only viable way to navigate the digital world without being fully consumed by self-loathing is to decide that all of the people who snipe at you from the sidelines aren’t really people at all. They’re more like ubiquitous wraiths — eyes looking at you from behind a painting, shadows that your subconscious might warp into an ominous shape, visions in the bog that almost lured Frodo to his death in “The Two Towers.” To let any of it in is to let all of it in, and there’s no amount of fame, money, or adulation that can fully inoculate sensitive people against the poison that seeps into their skin every time they pick up their phone (take it from me, someone who doesn’t have any of those things).

And so critics have gone from being a healthy part of the artistic ecosystem to something that artists feel like they need to be immunized against. Which isn’t to suggest that the animus between artists and critics is anything new. On the contrary, it’s as time-honored a cinematic tradition as popcorn at the movies or, say, the old trope of talented indie filmmakers who completely lose the plot once they become too successful.

If anything, that animus used to be a lot more personal, if only because it was expected that artists would know critics by name. Vincent Gallo famously called Roger Ebert a “fat pig with the physique of a slave trader” after Ebert panned “The Brown Bunny” at Cannes. Uwe Boll offered to box his biggest haters after he got sick of being a critical punching bag, and he beat the absolute shit out of all five of the people who took him up on it. Pauline Kael got so far under Clint Eastwood’s skin that he paid a psychiatrist to figure out what her problem was (the shrink naturally concluded that Kael just wanted to fuck Eastwood), while her review of “Ryan’s Daughter” caused David Lean such a crisis of confidence that he almost retired from directing altogether. And he made “Lawrence of Arabia”! (Which Kael also hated).

I’m not so bold as to presume that I — or any of my contemporaries — have a pen worthy of Kael’s poison or place in the public sphere, but the contrast is telling all the same. Instead of headline-making beefs that stand the test of time, today’s critics might be the subject of a petulant DM or a horde-summoning quote tweet. A prominent action director used to get drunk and send me crude messages about my wife via Instagram, but I think he’s sober now. Ron Perlman once called me a “cunt” on social media because I shat on some Christmas movie he made about furries, but I’d be shocked if he remembered that. Or really if he remembered “Pottersville” at all. I had a funny back-and-forth with a good-natured David Ayer after I trashed his Netflix debacle “Bright”; his promise to put my review on his fridge suggested a much less formal riff on Ridley Scott’s decision to frame Kael’s “Blade Runner” pan and hang it in his office. These days, film critics typically only get put on blast by name, at scale, when they make a major sociopolitical misstep of some kind, such as by arguing that a cartoon about red pandas somehow limits its scope by spotlighting Toronto’s immigrant community, or by fixating on the sexual possibilities that could be explored as a form of Mrs. Incredible’s superpowers. (Pixar movies are just irresistible rakes for critics to step on, I guess).

Today’s filmmakers and stars are certainly still aware of their alleged shooters (bracing for another “Dune” situation, Timothée Chalamet asked me to be kind to “Marty Supreme,” though I’m generally a fan, and he had nothing to fear in that case), but most publicly shared pushback is aimed at “the critics” writ large, if only so we can be reduced to cynical strawmen who exist in contrast to “the fans.” The marketing campaign for “Gotti” argued that critics “put out the hit” on the New York mob classic, and then asked people who they trusted more: themselves or “a troll behind a keyboard.” Ignoring the fact that this troll was behind his keyboard in a fucking tuxedo because that movie premiered as an unofficial selection at Cannes, the poptimistic notion that “real people love things” has become a go-to gameplan for an era where reality is easier to warp than it is to reckon with. In an ironic example of life imitating art, “Digger” recently adopted a similar approach.

I suspect that the systemic diminishment of arts criticism is both a cause and a symptom of this ever-worsening phenomenon. There was a time in this country when arts criticism was valued as a worthwhile pursuit unto itself, as opposed to a wonky and unreliable component of the promotional apparatus. The likes of Gore Vidal, James Baldwin, and Norman Mailer were regular fixtures on late night TV and panel shows; they were as famous as any of the people they wrote about, and when artists pushed back against their critics, it was seen as a debate between equals.

Because of that standing, the brightest minds of their generation were able to thrive as public intellectuals, and even invited to leverage their success into lucrative Hollywood careers of their own (as Vidal and Mailer both did before the resulting feud between them led to Mailer headbutting Vidal in the green room of “The Dick Cavett Show”). Today, the Vidals, Baldwins, and Mailers of the world would never belittle themselves by reviewing “Klara and the Sun” for $150, only for their work to be subsumed into a content aggregator that reduced it to a number in a larger set of numbers. In lieu of meaningful financial and intellectual compensation, any thinkers of such caliber today might understandably find arts criticism unworthy of their time and/or just share it to their Letterboxd for free.

That brings us to the reason why Waititi’s post was so excruciatingly tone-deaf, even though he’s hardly the first director to try the “Am I so out of touch? No, it’s the children who are wrong!” defense. The hierarchy of power in the discourse universe has grown as wildly lop-sided as the hierarchy of power in every other arena of public life. Even the most high-profile of critics are barely scraping by, while anyone successful enough to make news with a “the critics put out the hit” post is likely to be a millionaire several times over.

You’d have to be completely disconnected from reality not to recognize how gauche and myopic it is to call journalists of any kind “obsolete” for speaking truth to power and/or product, but I suppose that’s a side effect of spending 15 years in an ecosystem designed to protect itself at all costs. It’s an ecosystem supported by influencer screenings, celebrity interview podcasts, and so many other quality-laundering tactics that it feels like a desperate and radical act when a star like Tom Cruise dares to sit down with a real magazine writer. Only in an ecosystem like that could someone sharp and humane enough to direct “Boy” and the funny parts of “Thor: Ragnarok” become convinced that everyone who hated “Klara and the Sun” did so out of resentment for their own shortcomings. Only in an ecosystem like that could someone that sharp make a movie like “Klara and the Sun” at all. (Which is not to specifically denigrate the actual “Klara and the Sun,” which again I have not seen.)

Of course, it’s not Waititi’s fault that he’s a product of his time, and in light of Aaron Sorkin’s considerably more sensible and self-effacing response to the reviews for “The Social Reckoning,” it’s worth considering whether his relative grace has something to do with the fact that he first came to success during an earlier iteration of Hollywood, where perspective was easier to come by. Whatever the case, we’re all trying our best to protect ourselves in the face of a world where imitated humanity is of limitless value, and actual humanity is an Achilles’ heel — a world in which one of the great modern authors might be moved to write a fairy tale-like story that questions the distance that has grown between people as a result of our efforts to create external vessels for our souls.

Reading Waititi’s tactless Instagram post back for what I pray is the last time, I’m reminded of a resonant line from Ishiguro’s novel, a line that unsurprisingly failed to make it into Waititi’s adaptation: “What was becoming clear to me was the extent to which humans, in their wish to escape loneliness, made maneuvers that were very complex and hard to fathom.” Perhaps, in some abstract way, Waititi’s Instagram post captured the essence of “Klara and the Sun” better than his film ever could.

entry.title: Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break
entry.summary: To snag lead in Peter Farrelly's "I Play Rocky," the breakout tells IndieWire how he followed the iconoclastic actor and filmmaker's playbook.
entry.content:
I don’t think I was supposed to hear Anthony Ippolito when he exclaimed, “20 minutes?” right before this interview, as he was given the amount of time this interview would last. Though, it kind of hit me, if you’re not used to doing interviews — and there’s no way Ippolito can be at this young stage of his career — 20 minutes is a long time to make conversation with a total stranger. Especially, as he is quick to point out, after a barrage of quick, three-minute interviews.

Ippolito has been in films and television before — kind of famously now, he played Al Pacino in “The Offer” — but none of those were roles in which he’d have to do press. Let alone playing the lead role in a major motion picture in which everyone wants to talk to him. Oh, and that lead role is as … Sylvester Stallone.

Related Stories
‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement
AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them

In “I Play Rocky,” yes, Ippolito plays Stallone at the make or break point in Stallone’s career. Stallone had written “Rocky,” a very in-demand script. Not in demand was the idea of Stallone playing Rocky — as MGM offers more and more money to Stallone in an effort to get him to not play Rocky. (If you don’t know, Stallone stuck to his guns, played Rocky, and is now a very wealthy and famous actor.)

Directed by Peter Farrelly, Ippolito says he sent in multiple tapes trying to land this role — which does seem to be in the same spirit as the film itself. Though, Ippolito said, when he was actually going through the casting process, that’s not at all what he was thinking, even though it may seem that way now.

Ahead, he tells us (yes, over the course of 20 minutes) the Stallone movies he used to prep for playing Stallone, what is was like to talk to Stallone before filming, and why he loves Stallone and Dolly Parton together in “Rhinestone.” Also, if he had to play Stallone again in another movie, he does have another “I Play” installment in mind…

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Anthony Ippolito: 20 minutes?

IndieWire: You seem excited about this being 20 minutes?

It’s a little strange, I’ve been having three-minute increment conversations with somebody. So, yes, I am excited.

OK, so how many Stallone movies did you watch? Did you stick to that era? His voice kind of evolves by the late ‘80s.

Yeah, I really tried to stay focused on a period of time. I don’t know the exact number. More so, from the stuff I was looking at I was watching it over and over again, rewatching. With the exception of a few.

Like what?

Well, “Rocky Balboa.” It’s one of the best movies of the franchise.

For people who haven’t seen that one in a while, it’s very sweet.

It really is. It really is. And he does some excellent work in it. And I think it’s really powerful that he was able to come back many years later, after the fifth one, and make this incredible movie.

From closer to the “Rocky” era, I kind of love him in “The Prisoner of Second Avenue.” Jack Lemmon thinks he stole his wallet…

Yes!

It’s just scene after scene of Jack Lemmon chasing Stallone through Central Park trying to get his wallet back…

Just a little bit.

But then Jack Lemmon realizes he left his wallet at home and wound up being the one who mugged Stallone.

But he was mistaken for a mugger and this was part of his issue, right?

It’s funny watching it now, because it’s so obviously Sylvester Stallone. So it’s amusing the whole role is just him being chased.

I agree with you and I found that throughout a lot of the stuff I was unearthing throughout this process.

In that, if he hadn’t become famous, I’d still look at him and think, “what an interesting looking dude,” and wonder what happened to him.

And now we know.

Speaking of that, there were times during “I Play Rocky,” knowing full well what happens in real life, and I’m still like, “Maybe just take the money. That’s a lot.”

It’s really remarkable. Especially when you convert the amount from what it was then to what it would be now.

I know you made a video for your audition which involved an old punching bag and gloves. What were you saying in it?

Oh, well, there was certain dialogue I was coming up with, or thinking of coming up with. And I hadn’t had my hands on too much of the script at this point. So I was just trying to capture his physicality and his movement as a boxer. I was just really passionate about the project. I wanted to put myself out there in a way. And, thankfully, I was able to get my hands on the script a bit later on.

So are you doing lines from “Rocky”? Or just stuff you came up with on your own?

I toyed with a lot of stuff…

I ask because that’s a time when you haven’t gained the weight yet, so you’re not in the physical condition you are when filming. So I feel you had to really sell this dialogue? Which obviously worked.

Yeah, I mean … it was difficult to come up with that part of it. I had given myself inspiration with some parts of the original film, and some parts from what I felt would work for dialogue from what I was understanding of the story. And then once I was able to get the script, then I was able to just put scenes on tape. And then continuously send them stuff until they relented.

Oh, there was more than one? You just kept going?

Ohhhh, yeah.

Well, that’s the spirit of this movie. Did you feel that way when you were sending them in? “Well, that’s what Stallone did.”

Hm … maybe? You know, it seems that way kind of now?

Now that it’s worked out.

Right. But at that time, I was just like, “I probably seem crazy to everyone who is on the other end of this.”

See, just like Stallone.

Yeah, but I wasn’t thinking about that part for some reason, I guess.

Which is probably good, if you were getting ahead of yourself it doesn’t work out the way it did?

Yeah, you’re probably right.

I know you spoke to Stallone before filming. A year ago, he was saying he knew nothing about this movie. When and how did that change?

Peter Farrelly tells a funny story about that. He had actually met with Stallone prior to that and discussed his level of involvement. And they discussed how Stallone would kind of not be necessarily in the trenches with us, just for the sake of Peter not wanting people to feel like Stallone had his hand in it in a way that it was shaped…

And historically Stallone never does that. I say that sarcastically because I’m well aware he has a specific vision for any movie he’s involved in…

Right. Right. So, Stallone went back after that and told somebody he has no idea about it. And Peter was like, “What are you doing?” And Stallone said, “You told me to separate myself.” And Peter was like, “Not that far, man!” So, I guess that was just a bit of a communication breakdown.

So in Stallone’s mind, he was doing a favor by saying that?

I’m not sure, but I was able to speak with him about a month before we started shooting. And I’m very grateful he was willing to take the time

What was that like? Was he in good spirits or was he apprehensive?

He was in great spirits about it. I was nervous, as you could probably imagine.

I met him once. He can be intimidating.

Yeah, and not only that, I had done so much of my own research. So, up to that point, it was really built up as this really big thing in my head. So, I was just really, really excited to meet him and to listen to him. He was really, really generous and disarming and very willing to share what that period of time was like for him.

What did he tell you that you don’t know already?

Oh, man. Well, he discussed with me building the character of Rocky as a writer. That’s where it became really interesting to me. Because he had studied filmmaking and writing while being an usher. So, hearing his perspective and his kind of clinical breakdown of how he approaches a script and of a character? It was hugely informative in developing and my understanding of this side of him as a writer.

From that, what changed on how you approached playing him? How does that conversation inform what we see?

You just really understand that this thing is his baby. And it really makes more sense that these numbers going so high during these negotiations because the script is that good. And so well written. Yeah, he’s a terrific writer and I think he proved that to Chartoff and Winkler with “Paradise Alley,” first.

My only experience with him was at the afterparty for “The Family Stallone.” He shows up at this restaurant in Little Italy and it’s like the Red Sea parting. Everyone stopped talking and made room so he could walk by. When he got near me I said, “Hey, Sly,” which I immediately regretted. He stopped, looked at me, and gave me a little nod.

A little nod!

He then walked off and I thought, “You know, good enough.”

Are you glad that you said it now? I feel like I would be.

I am. He acknowledged I existed.

That’s cool.

But you keep bringing up meeting Wim Wenders. I know you’re a fan of his, is there something maybe happening?

I got to meet him at the Zurich Film Festival.

I know you like his movies, are you going to work with him?

I just think he makes great films, he’s made great films and he was a really, really sweet man and we got to speak. That’s pretty much it.

What other filmmakers do you like?

I feel that way about so many. Well, Scorsese obviously. Richard Linklater, Derek Cianfrance, Tim Burton.

That’s an eclectic group. “Place Beyond the Pines” and “Beetlejuice” are very different movies.

Very different movies. Well, I like that, You can go in so many different directions. And I appreciate directors and filmmakers who are singular.

And that is kind of the thing about Stallone, too. Did you look at the movies Stallone directed?

Honestly, well, I know he directed all the “Rocky” movies other than the first and fifth ones. And I understand he directed more stuff past that as well. But I hadn’t specifically looked at stuff he directed for this.

How far back did you go back to watch with Peter Farrelly’s films? Did you go back to “Dumb & Dumber”?

I’ve seen so much of his stuff already. So there’s not one that jumped out at me, but also, obviously, “There’s Something About Mary.”

It’s still so funny…

It really is. I think he really killed it with that one. I mean, he has such an incredible sensibility. And he’s always aware of something on set. If there’s a moment to be discovered, to make a meal out of it, he’ll find it.

I always think about, “Unless someone comes up with six-minute abs.”

“No, seven. Not six.”

On social media a lot of people are doing their own “I Play …,” then insert any other Stallone movie type posts. If you had to play him again, what movie would you want to do?

Oh, man.

Like, “I Play Cobra,” would be interesting. I do love “Cobra.”

You know, I guess I’m not the right age for this, but “I Play Rocky Balboa” would be very interesting…

That’s the first one you saw, right?

Well, it’s the first one I remember. I would have had to have seen the ones prior? To the point I’m in the theater for “Rocky Balboa.”

Well, not necessarily. The first one I saw was “Rocky III”…

Oh, really? OK then.

Because it was the one on cable all the time. Then I was told, “Oh, you know, the first one is a lot different.”

Yeah, I was pretty young, but I do remember seeing “Rocky Balboa.” And I just think there’s something interesting about the fact that, similar to how he’s fighting the boxing commission at the time to let him fight, because they think that he can’t, or shouldn’t — I think he was having a similar dialogue with the studio at the time. About him making the movie in the first place.

It’s interesting, even at that point, they still didn’t think they could take a chance on him making a “Rocky” movie.

I guess, yeah. It’s strange, but history does repeat itself.

Have you seen “Rhinestone”?

Of course.

Ah, OK, it’s not streaming, so it’s a little harder to find. It’s just interesting this is only a few years after “Rocky” and now he’s on stage singing with Dolly Parton. It’s kind of fascination what that one decision did for him…

It’s very true. And I think Dolly Parton is spectacular in that.

Oh, I agree.

How good is she in that? Right? I mean, she has such a warmth to her. I mean, yeah. She’s just incredible in the movie and it makes it so fun. The two of them! They are dynamic.

You could also make “I Play Nick Martinelli.”

We’ll see.

So what are the lessons you personally took away from playing Stallone? I can’t help but think there are lessons here for actors starting out.

I agree. Well, he really overcame so much and he didn’t have too many people in his corner at the time. I mean, thankfully, he had Sasha who was there for him, who AnnaSophia Robb plays in the movie. And she’s so great in it. And as much as you want to see Stallone persevere, and be kind of a lone wolf through this? For actors there’s meaning in that, and there’s a lesson to be learned in that.

But there’s also a lesson to be found in Sasha. Because you need that person sometimes in your life. Or sometimes it’s good to be that person for people — to remind people to believe in themselves. Because, no matter what, Stallone overcame so much, but of course he doubted himself. And if you don’t have at least somebody who is there, willing to be that person to remind you to believe in yourself, it’s a tough road.

See, we did 20 minutes, it wasn’t bad.

No, no, not bad at all.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “I Play Rocky” in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.

entry.title: ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement
entry.summary: Yoju Matsubayashi's latest film follows third-generation Okinawan-Brazilian as they reflect on their distant homeland.
entry.content:
The Kasato Maru ferried 325 Okinawans to Brazil in 1908, making it the first immigrant ship from Japan to do so. That history is highlighted by the opening of the documentary “Okinawa Saudade,” (“saudade” being a Portuguese word for bittersweet longing, typically around a memory or place). The film looks at the results a century later, now that an estimated 200,000 Brazilians of Okinawan descent are living in Brazil today, and director and cinematographer Yoju Matsubayashi finds a specific and emotionally straightforward route into complicated history. The director has covered the subject to some extent before in 2020’s “Okinawa / Santos,” a film which collected testimony on the forced deportation and even internment of Japanese immigrants in Brazil in the 1940s.””Okinawa Saudade”” narrows that focus to the families of two third-generation Okinawan-Brazilians, specifically ones with an interest in — and a longing towards — the island their families came from, something partially explored through the arts.

Related Stories
AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them
The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

A visual motif of waves viewed from above punctuates different segments of the film, typically as its subject reflect on the previous movements of their families. In the first instance of the shot, a dissolve to a young girl practicing a traditional Japanese dance on her family’s farm in Brazil immediately communicates that feeling of “saudade,” a soft and gently expressed shadow hanging over much of the film. That feeling of “saudade” is seen in the incidental details the director chooses to include, like how one subject’s grandfather grew dragonfruit with Okinawan seeds, as well as his capturing of more outwardly emotional moments, like a tearful reaction to photos not seen in a long time.

The teenage girl Yumi practices Ryukyu Buyo, while a man named Everton practices Eisa, an Okinawan folk dance involving drums. By unspooling their enthusiasm for the history of such Okinawan heritage arts and the history of their families, Matsubayashi also orbits a history of displacement. This emerges in an accumulation of lots of small personal stories, like how one characters recounts their family’s war-motivated exile from Santos. Yumi and Everton also learn more of these details for themselves, the film following them on their travels to Okinawa through exchange programs and traineeships. (In some delightful cases, the learning cuts both ways, as Everton reunites with estranged family, and Yumi’s Okinawan relative marvels at the dialect being preserved halfway around the world.)

Capturing their subjects’ respective journeys with occasional and mostly spontaneous interviews, Matsubayashi prioritizes personal histories over the big picture,as the assembly of the footage and the occasional interjection of archival material makes the relationship of this diaspora a bit clearer. Some of these families left Okinawa to avoid the military draft as well as starvation. Others were divided because of land seizures by the US military in the wake of the war (“I’ve learned that this is a sad place,” Yumi reflects, a quote placed over footage of lingering American military bases on the island). Some viewers might be dissatisfied with how Matsubayashi never quite engages with World War II and the full history of Okinawan annexation directly, but the context feels like plenty for the stories which he is telling, choosing instead to focus on the feelings which all children of immigrant backgrounds have felt: an uncertainty about their connection with the homeland of their parents and grandparents, and a yearning to understand it. The glimpses are enough, as “Okinawa Saudade”gradually paints a picture of how the historical struggles of the island have translated to the diaspora.

Everton outright says why he engages in Eisa drumming, saying that “we are Brazilians, but we don’t look like Brazilians, so we are always looking for belonging,” and his engagement with these traditional artforms becomes a part of this. Both learn the different nuances of their respective practices at home compared to in Okinawa, though both are graced with teachers who refuse to be super didactic about what is “authentic” (“We are always adjusting,” Yumi’s teacher says, “there is no such thing as perfection”). It’s also simply moving seeing, through Matsubayashi’s rather unvarnished camerawork, how the connections and feelings embodied in performing arts can have such far reach across time and place, highlighting the community found by the Brazilian Okinawans who preserved a little piece of the island for themselves.

Grade: B+

“Okinawa Saudade” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

entry.title: AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them
entry.summary: A week after partnering on our Future of Filmmaking Summit, AT&T and IndieWire teamed up again to celebrate the next generation of storytellers.
entry.content:
IndieWire and AT&T spent the month of October demonstrating our shared commitment to championing filmmakers and bringing untold stories to life.

First up was the IndieWire Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles, presented by AT&T, which assembled artists, executives, and thought leaders from every corner of the entertainment industry for a day of programming about where Hollywood is heading. Then a week later, we partnered to present the Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest, which celebrated the next generation of filmmakers who are bringing their visions to life.

Held at Ovation Hollywood on Saturday, October 25, the Filmmaker Party brought directors and festival attendees together for an evening of networking and movie discussions. The party even featured a complimentary headshot booth for anyone who wanted to take their career to the next level.

Related Stories
The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever
‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Is Lured Into Lily James’ Cult in a Gut-Wrenching Drama

The event was attended by “Honeyjoon” director Lilian Mehrel, who made her debut feature with the $1 million prize she won from the 2024 AT&T Untold Stories competition. She explained how the competition, which awards the biggest prize of its kind in the world, empowered her to tell a story that might not have otherwise found a home in the industry.

“Thank you to AT&T, to AFI Fest, and to everyone who champions filmmakers,” she said. “Because of you, more untold stories become told.”

Her comments echoed those of “Color Book” director David Fortune, who attended the Future of Filmmaking Summit to share his own experience from the life-changing competition.

Keep reading to see all the photos from the 2026 AFI Filmmaker Party, presented by AT&T and IndieWire.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen.
